q: Q1. (MCQ) A point charge +Q is at the centre of a spherical Gaussian surface of radius R. If the radius is doubled, the flux will: (A) halve (B) double (C) remain the same (D) become four times. [SQP; similar 2015]
a: Answer: (C). Flux = q(enclosed)/ε0. It does not depend on size or shape of the closed surface.

q: Q2. (1 mark) What is the electric flux through a cube of side 1 cm which encloses an electric dipole? [2015]
a: Answer: Zero, because net charge enclosed = +q − q = 0.

q: Q3. (2 marks) Define electric flux. Is it scalar or vector? Give its SI unit. [2018]
a: Answer: Electric flux through a surface = number of field lines crossing it = ∮ E·dA (= EA cos θ for uniform field). It is a scalar. Unit: N m² C^-1 (or V m).

q: Q4. (Derivation, 3–5 marks) Derive the electric field of a dipole at a point on its axial line. Show that for r >> a, E = 2p / (4πε0 r³). [2015, 2017]
a:
Steps:

  1. Dipole: −q at A, +q at B, AB = 2a, p = q × 2a (from −q to +q). Point P on axis at distance r from centre O, on the side of +q.
  2. Field due to +q: E+ = kq/(r − a)², directed away from +q (along p).
  3. Field due to −q: E− = kq/(r + a)², directed towards −q (opposite to p).
  4. Net E = kq [1/(r − a)² − 1/(r + a)²] = kq × 4ar / (r² − a²)².
  5. E = k × 2p r / (r² − a²)², along p.
  6. For r >> a: E = 2kp / r³ = 2p / (4πε0 r³). Direction: along p. Diagram: straight line with −q, O, +q, and P to the right; arrows E+ (right) bigger than E− (left).

q: Q5. (Derivation, 3–5 marks) Derive the field at a point on the equatorial line of a dipole. [2019, 2023; 2025 asked field at (0, y) for charges at (±a, 0)]
a:
Steps:

  1. P on perpendicular bisector at distance r from O. Distance from each charge = √(r² + a²).
  2. Magnitudes: E+ = E− = kq/(r² + a²).
  3. Components perpendicular to the axis cancel. Components parallel to the axis add (both point from +q side towards −q side, i.e. opposite to p).
  4. E = 2 E+ cos θ, with cos θ = a/√(r² + a²).
  5. E = kq × 2a / (r² + a²)^(3/2) = kp / (r² + a²)^(3/2), direction opposite to p.
  6. For r >> a: E = p / (4πε0 r³). (Half of axial value. If distance is halved, E becomes 8 times – 2023 part.)

q: Q6. (3 marks) Write the torque on a dipole in a uniform field. Show stable and unstable equilibrium. [2017; SQP-type]
a: Answer: τ = p × E, magnitude τ = pE sin θ. Net force on dipole in uniform field = 0. Stable: p parallel to E (θ = 0°), τ = 0. Unstable: p antiparallel (θ = 180°), τ = 0. Maximum torque pE at θ = 90°.

q: Q7. (Numerical, 2 marks) A dipole: −1.0 pC at (0, 0) and +1.0 pC at (3 mm, 4 mm). Field E = 1000 V/m along +x is switched on. Find the torque. [2024]
Q8. (Derivation, 3 marks) Using Gauss's law find E due to an infinitely long straight wire of linear charge density λ. Draw E vs r graph. [2018; 2026 used it for force between two line charges]
a:
Steps:

  1. Gaussian surface: cylinder of radius r, length l, coaxial with wire.
  2. Flux through flat ends = 0 (E parallel to them). Flux through curved surface = E × 2πrl.
  3. Charge enclosed = λl. Gauss: E × 2πrl = λl/ε0.
  4. E = λ / (2πε0 r), radially outward for λ > 0. Graph: E vs r is a falling curve (E ∝ 1/r), like a hyperbola.

q: Q9. (Derivation, 3 marks) Using Gauss's law, find E due to an infinite plane sheet of charge density σ. [2016, 2017]
a: Steps: Take a cylinder (pillbox) of cross-section A crossing the sheet. Flux only through the two flat faces: EA + EA = 2EA. Charge enclosed = σA. So 2EA = σA/ε0 → E = σ / (2ε0), perpendicular to sheet, away for +σ, towards for −σ. E does not depend on distance.

q: Q10. (Derivation, 3 marks) Field due to a uniformly charged thin spherical shell (radius R, charge q) (i) outside (r > R) (ii) inside (r < R). [2025; 2026 (shell flux parts)]
a:
Steps:

  1. Outside: Gaussian sphere of radius r > R. E × 4πr² = q/ε0 → E = q / (4πε0 r²) (as if all charge at centre).
  2. Inside: Gaussian sphere r < R encloses no charge → E × 4πr² = 0 → E = 0.
  3. Graph: E = 0 up to R, jumps to maximum at R, then falls as 1/r².

q: Q11. (Numerical, 3 marks) Electric field E = 500x î N/C (x in m). A cube of side 0.1 m has its faces at x = 0.1 m and x = 0.2 m (other faces parallel to the x-axis). Find the flux through the cube and charge inside. [2024 – figure positions assumed here as above]
a:
Steps:

  1. Only the two faces perpendicular to x have flux. Area A = 0.01 m².
  2. At x = 0.1 m: E = 50 N/C, flux in = −50 × 0.01 = −0.5 N m²/C.
  3. At x = 0.2 m: E = 100 N/C, flux out = +100 × 0.01 = +1.0 N m²/C.
  4. Net flux = 0.5 N m²/C.
  5. q = ε0 × flux = 8.854 × 10^-12 × 0.5 ≈ 4.4 × 10^-12 C.

q: Q12. (Numerical, 2 marks) Two charges +q and +q are a distance d apart. How much work is needed to bring another +q from infinity to the midpoint? [SQP]
a: Steps: Potential at midpoint V = kq/(d/2) + kq/(d/2) = 4kq/d. Work W = qV = 4kq²/d = q² / (πε0 d).

q: Q13. (Derivation, 3 marks) Derive the potential due to a dipole at a point on its axis; show V = p / (4πε0 r²) for r >> a. [2019; 2024 (far point)]
a: Steps: V = kq/(r − a) − kq/(r + a) = kq × 2a/(r² − a²) = kp/(r² − a²). For r >> a, V = kp/r² = p/(4πε0 r²). On the equatorial line V = 0 (equal and opposite contributions).

q: Q14. (Derivation, 3 marks) Derive the potential energy of a dipole in a uniform field. When is it maximum and minimum? [2024]
a:
Steps:

  1. Torque τ = pE sin θ. Work to rotate from θ0 to θ: W = ∫ pE sin θ dθ = pE (cos θ0 − cos θ).
  2. Take θ0 = 90° as zero energy: U(θ) = −pE cos θ = −p·E.
  3. Minimum U = −pE at θ = 0° (stable). Maximum U = +pE at θ = 180° (unstable).

q: Q15. (2 marks) Define equipotential surface. Draw them for (i) a point charge (ii) uniform field along z. Why is E always perpendicular to them? [2016, 2019]
a: Answer: Surface where potential is the same at every point. (i) concentric spheres around the charge, getting farther apart outward. (ii) equally spaced planes parallel to the x-y plane. No work is done moving a charge on it (ΔV = 0), so E has no component along the surface; E ⟂ surface.

q: Q16. (Numerical, 2 marks) How will you connect 6 μF, 9 μF and 18 μF capacitors to get (i) minimum (ii) maximum capacitance? [SQP]
a: Steps: (i) Series: 1/C = 1/6 + 1/9 + 1/18 = (3 + 2 + 1)/18 = 1/3 → C = 3 μF (minimum). (ii) Parallel: C = 6 + 9 + 18 = 33 μF (maximum).

q: Q17. (MCQ) Ten capacitors of 1 μF each are joined in parallel to 100 V. Total energy stored = ? [2024]
Q18. (Numerical, 3 marks) Two capacitors C1 and C2, first in series then in parallel across 100 V, store 0.045 J and 0.25 J. Find C1 and C2 and charge on each in parallel. [2015]
a:
Steps:

  1. Parallel: ½(C1 + C2)(100)² = 0.25 → C1 + C2 = 5 × 10^-5 F = 50 μF.
  2. Series: ½ C1C2/(C1 + C2)² = 0.045 → C1C2/(C1 + C2) = 9 μF → C1C2 = 450 (μF)².
  3. Solve x² − 50x + 450 = 0 → x = 38.2 μF and 11.8 μF.
  4. Charges (parallel, V = 100 V): Q = CV → 3.82 × 10^-3 C and 1.18 × 10^-3 C.

q: Q19. (2 marks) What factors does the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor depend on? Why can an isolated conductor not have a large capacitance? [SQP]
a: Answer: C = Kε0A/d → depends on plate area A, separation d (C ∝ 1/d), and dielectric constant K of medium. Isolated sphere C = 4πε0R; even a sphere as big as the Earth has only about 711 μF, so a single conductor cannot have large C.

q: Q20. (Numerical, 2 marks) Show E = −dV/dr. Air breaks down at 2.5 × 10^6 V/m. A metal sphere must reach 5 × 10^5 V. Minimum radius? [SQP]
a: Steps: Work done moving unit charge by dr against E: dV = −E dr → E = −dV/dr. For a sphere, V = kQ/R and E = kQ/R² → E = V/R. R = V/E = 5 × 10^5 / 2.5 × 10^6 = 0.2 m.

q: Q21. (Numerical, 2 marks) Two isolated metal spheres of radii 1 cm and 3 cm have the same surface charge density 10^-9 C/m². They are joined by a thin wire. Find the new charge on the smaller sphere. [2024; 2016 similar idea]
a:
Steps:

  1. Q1 = σ × 4πr1² = 10^-9 × 4π × 10^-4 = 4π × 10^-13 C; Q2 = 10^-9 × 4π × 9 × 10^-4 = 36π × 10^-13 C. Total Q = 40π × 10^-13 C.
  2. After joining, potentials equal: Q1'/r1 = Q2'/r2 → Q1' : Q2' = 1 : 3.
  3. Q1' = Q/4 = 10π × 10^-13 ≈ 3.14 × 10^-12 C. (Charge flows from the larger sphere to the smaller, since with equal σ the larger sphere is at higher potential.)

q: Q22. (Derivation, 3 marks) Derive the relation I = neAvd. Also derive vd = eEτ/m. [2016, 2026]
a:
Steps:

  1. Electron acceleration a = −eE/m. Averaged over relaxation time τ: vd = −eEτ/m (magnitude eEτ/m).
  2. In time Δt, electrons in length vdΔt cross area A: number = n A vd Δt; charge = neAvdΔt.
  3. I = charge/time = neAvd. (2026 part: if length doubled at same V, E = V/l halves, so vd halves.)

q: Q23. (Derivation, 3 marks) Show j = σE with σ = ne²τ/m, and resistivity ρ = m/(ne²τ). [2018, 2024, 2025]
a: Steps: j = I/A = nevd = ne(eEτ/m) = (ne²τ/m)E. So σ = ne²τ/m and ρ = 1/σ = m/(ne²τ). Current density is a vector; unit A/m².

q: Q24. (Numerical, 2 marks) At what temperature will a silver wire have twice its resistance at 20 °C? α = 4.0 × 10^-3 /K. [2024]
Q25. (MCQ) Cell's open-circuit pd is 8 V; it falls to 4 V when 4 A is drawn. Internal resistance = ? [2023]
Q26. (Numerical, 2 marks) A battery of emf 21 V, internal resistance 3 Ω gives 3 A through a resistor. Find (i) resistor (ii) terminal voltage. [2026]
Q27. (Numerical, 3 marks) With R = 4 Ω the current is 1 A; with R = 9 Ω it is 0.5 A. Find E and r. Draw V vs I. [2015]
a: Steps: E = 1(4 + r) and E = 0.5(9 + r). So 4 + r = 4.5 + 0.5r → r = 1 Ω, E = 5 V. Graph: V = E − Ir is a straight line falling from V = E (at I = 0) with slope −r.

q: Q28. (Numerical, 2 marks) Battery 12 V, r = 2 Ω, connected to 4 Ω. Show voltmeter across cell and across resistor read the same. Why is voltmeter in parallel and ammeter in series? [2016; 2017 similar]
a: Steps: I = 12/(4 + 2) = 2 A. Across resistor: 2 × 4 = 8 V. Across cell: 12 − 2 × 2 = 8 V. Same. Ammeter has very low resistance (does not change current); voltmeter has very high resistance (draws almost no current).

q: Q29. (Derivation, 3 marks) Using Kirchhoff's rules, get the balance condition of a Wheatstone bridge. [2015, 2024; 2026 A-R; SQP MCQ]
a:
Steps:

  1. Arms P (AB), Q (BC), R (AD), S (DC); galvanometer between B and D; cell across A and C.
  2. At balance Ig = 0, so current I1 in P and Q, I2 in R and S.
  3. Loop ABDA: −I1P + I2R = 0 (Ig = 0) → I1P = I2R.
  4. Loop BCDB: −I1Q + I2S = 0 → I1Q = I2S.
  5. Divide: P/Q = R/S. (Swapping cell and galvanometer does not change balance.) Kirchhoff rules: Junction rule – sum of currents at a junction = 0 (charge conservation). Loop rule – sum of emfs = sum of IR drops in a closed loop (energy conservation).

q: Q30. (MCQ) Bulbs rated 200 V–60 W and 200 V–100 W. Ratio R1/R2 = ? [SQP]
Q31. (MCQ) Two identical heaters (1000 W, 220 V) in parallel across 220 V. Total power? [SQP]
a: Answer: Each works at rated voltage, P = 1000 + 1000 = 2000 W.

q: Q32. (2 marks) Bulbs P and Q have resistances in ratio 1 : 2 and are in series. Ratio of powers? [2018]
a: Answer: Same current in series, P = I²R → PP : PQ = 1 : 2. (In parallel it would be 2 : 1, since P = V²/R.)

q: Q33. (2 marks) Describe the path of free electrons in a conductor (a) with an electric field (b) without it. [SQP]
a: Answer: (a) Random zig-zag motion with collisions, plus a slow net drift opposite to E → current flows. (b) Only random thermal motion in all directions; average velocity zero → no current.

q: Q34. (Derivation, 3 marks) Using Biot–Savart law, find B at the centre of a circular loop of radius R carrying I (and state B on the axis). [2016, 2017, 2023; 2025 asked vector form]
a:
Steps:

  1. Biot–Savart: dB = (μ0/4π) I (dl × r) / r³, magnitude dB = (μ0/4π) I dl sin θ / r².
  2. At centre, every element is at distance R and dl ⟂ r (θ = 90°), all dB in the same direction.
  3. B = (μ0/4π)(I/R²) × ∮dl = (μ0/4π)(I/R²)(2πR) = μ0I / (2R).
  4. On the axis at distance x: B = μ0IR² / [2(R² + x²)^(3/2)], along the axis (right-hand thumb rule). Diagram: loop with field lines passing through centre like a small bar magnet.

q: Q35. (MCQ) A long wire with a semicircular loop of radius 10 cm carries 5 A. B at centre of the semicircle? [SQP]
a: Answer: B = μ0I/(4R) = 4π × 10^-7 × 5/(4 × 0.1) = 5π × 10^-6 T = 5π μT. (Straight parts pass through the centre line, so give zero.)

q: Q36. (2 marks) State Ampere's circuital law and use it to find B due to a long straight wire. [syllabus; 2015 used Ampere's law]
a: Answer: ∮B·dl = μ0 I(enclosed). Take a circle of radius r around the wire: B × 2πr = μ0I → B = μ0I/(2πr). Field lines are concentric circles (2025 MCQ).

q: Q37. (Numerical, 3 marks) A proton (KE 1.3384 × 10^-14 J) moving horizontally north to south enters B = 2.0 mT pointing east. q/m = 1.0 × 10^8 C/kg. Find (a) speed (b) acceleration (c) radius. [2024]

Q38. (Numerical, 3 marks) An alpha particle (m = 6.4 × 10^-27 kg, q = 3.2 × 10^-19 C) of energy 8.0 MeV enters B = 0.5 T at right angles. Find radius. When does it move in a helix / go undeviated? [2026]
a:
Steps:

  1. K = 8 × 1.6 × 10^-13 = 1.28 × 10^-12 J.
  2. p = √(2mK) = √(2 × 6.4 × 10^-27 × 1.28 × 10^-12) = 1.28 × 10^-19 kg m/s.
  3. r = p/(qB) = 1.28 × 10^-19 / (3.2 × 10^-19 × 0.5) = 0.8 m.
  4. Helix: velocity at an angle (not 0°, 90°, 180°) to B. Undeviated: velocity parallel or antiparallel to B (F = qvB sin θ = 0).

q: Q39. (2 marks) Find the condition for a charged particle to pass undeviated through crossed E and B fields (velocity selector). [2017]
a: Answer: v, E and B mutually perpendicular with electric and magnetic forces opposite. qE = qvB → v = E/B. Only particles with this speed go straight.

q: Q40. (Numerical, 3 marks) Two long parallel wires A and B, 2.5 cm apart, carry 5.0 A and 2.5 A in opposite directions. Find force on 10 cm of wire B. Define 1 ampere. [2023; 2019, 2024 A-R similar]
a: Steps: F = μ0 I1 I2 L / (2πd) = 2 × 10^-7 × 5 × 2.5 × 0.1 / 0.025 = 1.0 × 10^-5 N, repulsive (opposite currents repel; like currents attract). 1 ampere: the current which, flowing in two infinitely long parallel wires 1 m apart in vacuum, produces a force of 2 × 10^-7 N per metre length on each.

q: Q41. (Numerical, 3 marks) A coil of 30 turns, radius 8.0 cm, carries 6 A in a horizontal B = 1.0 T. Field lines make 30° with the plane of the coil. Find the torque. What if the coil is of irregular shape with same area? [2026; NCERT]
a: Steps: Angle between B and normal (area vector) = 90° − 30° = 60°. τ = NIAB sin 60° = 30 × 6 × π(0.08)² × 1 × 0.866 ≈ 3.1 N m. For any planar shape of the same area the torque is the same (τ depends only on area).

q: Q42. (Numerical, 3 marks) An ammeter of resistance 13 Ω reads up to 100 A. What shunt extends its range to 750 A? Why is the coil wound on a metal frame? [SQP]
a: Steps: Shunt carries 750 − 100 = 650 A, same pd as meter: 100 × 13 = 650 × S → S = 2 Ω. Metal frame: eddy currents in the frame damp the oscillations so the pointer comes to rest quickly (electromagnetic damping).

q: Q43. (MCQ) A galvanometer (resistance G) is converted to an ammeter of range I; galvanometer current is 0.1% of I. Resistance of the ammeter? [2024]
a: Answer: Ig = 0.001I. Shunt S = IgG/(I − Ig) = G/999. Ammeter resistance = GS/(G + S) = G/1000. Voltmeter conversion: high resistance R in series, R = V/Ig − G.

q: Q44. (2 marks) A material has relative permeability 800. Identify it and write two properties. [SQP]
a: Answer: μr >> 1 → ferromagnetic. Strongly attracted by magnets; retains magnetism (can make permanent magnets); shows hysteresis; becomes paramagnetic above Curie temperature.

q: Q45. (3 marks) Give three differences between dia-, para- and ferromagnetic substances with examples. [2019; 2016, 2018, 2025 similar] | Property | Dia | Para | Ferro | |---|---|---|---| | Behaviour near magnet | Weakly repelled | Weakly attracted | Strongly attracted | | Susceptibility χ | Small, negative | Small, positive | Very large, positive | | μr | Slightly < 1 | Slightly > 1 | Very large (>> 1) | | Field lines | Pushed out | Slightly concentrated | Strongly concentrated | | Temperature effect | Almost none | χ ∝ 1/T (Curie law) | Becomes para above Curie point | | Examples | Bismuth, copper, water | Aluminium, sodium, oxygen | Iron, cobalt, nickel |
Q46. (MCQ / A-R) Assertion: When a copper bar is placed in a magnetic field, field lines get concentrated inside it. Reason: Copper is paramagnetic. [2023]
a: Answer: (D) Both false. Copper is diamagnetic, so lines are pushed out of it.

q: Q47. (MCQ) A superconducting ball (cooled in liquid nitrogen) is placed near a bar magnet. It moves ______ and its magnetic moment is ______ the magnet's. [SQP]
a: Answer: Away from the magnet; opposite (a superconductor is a perfect diamagnet).

q: Q48. (2 marks) State Gauss's law for magnetism and its significance. [SQP; 2019]
a: Answer: Net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero: ∮B·dA = 0. Significance: isolated magnetic poles (monopoles) do not exist; magnetic field lines form closed loops.

q: Q49. (2 marks) State Faraday's laws and Lenz's law. Show Lenz's law follows conservation of energy. [2026; SQP]
a: Answer: Faraday: induced emf e = −dΦ/dt (N turns: −N dΦ/dt). Lenz: the induced current opposes the change that produces it. If a magnet's N-pole is pushed towards a coil, the near face becomes N and repels it; we must do work against this repulsion, and that work appears as electrical energy. If the current helped the motion, we would get energy for nothing – impossible.

q: Q50. (2 marks) A bar magnet falls through a metal ring. Why is its acceleration less than g? [SQP]
a: Answer: Changing flux induces a current in the ring. By Lenz's law this current opposes the motion (repels when approaching, attracts when leaving), so there is an upward force → a < g.

q: Q51. (Numerical, 1–2 marks) A square loop of side 50 cm is in B = 3.0 T perpendicular to its plane. It is rotated by 90° in 0.3 s. Average emf? [2026]
a: Steps: Φ initial = BA = 3 × 0.25 = 0.75 Wb; final = 0. e = ΔΦ/Δt = 0.75/0.3 = 2.5 V.

q: Q52. (Numerical, 2 marks) Current in a coil changes from 8.0 A to 2.0 A in 0.6 s; induced emf is 50 V. Find L. Write the dimensional formula of L. [2026]
a: Steps: e = L(ΔI/Δt) → 50 = L × (6/0.6) = 10L → L = 5 H. Dimensions: [M L² T^-2 A^-2].

q: Q53. (Derivation, 3 marks) Define mutual inductance. Derive M for two long coaxial solenoids of the same length l. [2015, 2017, 2023 (coil on solenoid)]
a:
Steps:

  1. Inner solenoid S1: n1 turns/m, area A1. Outer S2: n2 turns/m.
  2. Current I2 in S2 gives B2 = μ0n2I2 inside it.
  3. Flux linked with S1 (N1 = n1 l turns): N1Φ1 = n1 l × A1 × μ0n2I2.
  4. M = N1Φ1/I2 = μ0 n1 n2 A1 l. (M12 = M21 = M.) Unit: henry (H). Definition: M = flux linked with one coil per unit current in the other (or emf in one coil per unit rate of change of current in the other).

q: Q54. (3 marks) State the principle of an AC generator and derive e = NBAω sin ωt. [2016, 2017, 2018]
a: Steps: Principle – electromagnetic induction. A coil (N turns, area A) rotates with angular speed ω in uniform B. Flux Φ = NBA cos ωt. e = −dΦ/dt = NBAω sin ωt. Peak emf e0 = NBAω (= 2πf NBA).

q: Q55. (MCQ) An ac ammeter reads 10 A. Peak current = ? [2025]
a: Answer: Meter reads rms. I0 = √2 × Irms = 10√2 A.

q: Q56. (MCQ) A capacitor has reactance X. If C is doubled and frequency tripled, new reactance = ? [2024]
a: Answer: XC = 1/(2πfC) → new X = X/(2 × 3) = X/6.

q: Q57. (Derivation, 3–5 marks) Using a phasor diagram, get the impedance of a series LCR circuit and the resonance condition. [2023, 2025, 2026, SQP; 2019]
a:
Steps:

  1. Same current i = i0 sin ωt in all. VR in phase with i; VL leads i by 90°; VC lags i by 90°.
  2. Phasors: VR along i; (VL − VC) perpendicular.
  3. V² = VR² + (VL − VC)² → V = i √[R² + (XL − XC)²].
  4. Z = √[R² + (XL − XC)²], tan φ = (XL − XC)/R, XL = ωL, XC = 1/(ωC).
  5. Resonance: XL = XC → ω0 = 1/√(LC), f0 = 1/(2π√(LC)). Then Z = R (minimum), current maximum, circuit acts purely resistive, VL and VC are 180° out of phase.
  6. Use: radio tuning – changing C changes f0; the station whose frequency equals f0 gives maximum current (SQP). Graph: current vs ω rises to a sharp peak at ω0.

q: Q58. (Derivation, 3 marks) Derive average power in an ac circuit; show it is zero for an ideal inductor. [2024, 2016]
a: Steps: v = v0 sin ωt, i = i0 sin(ωt − φ). p = vi = v0i0 sin ωt sin(ωt − φ) = (v0i0/2)[cos φ − cos(2ωt − φ)]. Average of cos(2ωt − φ) over a cycle = 0. So P = Vrms Irms cos φ. Ideal inductor: φ = 90°, cos φ = 0 → P = 0 (wattless current). Power factor = cos φ = R/Z.

q: Q59. (Numerical, 3 marks) A lamp is designed for 110 V dc and 11 A. To run it on 220 V, 50 Hz ac, a coil is put in series. Find the inductance. [2024]
Q60. (Numerical, 3 marks) An inductor draws 1 A from 200 V dc but only 0.5 A from 200 V, 50 Hz ac. Why? Find L. [2019]
a: Steps: With dc, XL = 0, so R = 200 Ω. With ac, Z = 200/0.5 = 400 Ω. XL = √(400² − 200²) = √120000 ≈ 346 Ω. L = 346/(2π × 50) ≈ 1.1 H. Current falls because the inductor offers reactance to ac.

q: Q61. (3 marks) A bulb is in series with an inductor and an ac source. What happens to brightness if (i) an iron rod is put inside the coil (ii) a capacitor with XC = XL is added (iii) frequency is decreased? [2015, 2016, 2026]
a: Answer: (i) L increases → XL increases → current falls → dimmer. (ii) XL − XC = 0 → Z = R, maximum current → brightest. (iii) XL = 2πfL decreases → current increases → brighter.

q: Q62. (Long, 5 marks) Draw a labelled diagram of a step-up transformer, state its principle and working, and give three energy losses. Does it violate energy conservation? Numerical: Np = 200, Ns = 3000, Vp = 90 V, Is = 2.0 A; find Vs and Ip. [2024; 2015, 2016, 2018, 2019, SQP]
a:
Answer:

  • Diagram: soft iron laminated core, primary (few turns) connected to ac input, secondary (many turns) to output.
  • Principle: mutual induction – changing current in primary changes flux in core, which induces emf in secondary.
  • Relations: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np; ideal: VpIp = VsIs so Ip/Is = Ns/Np.
  • Losses: (1) copper loss (I²R heating of windings), (2) eddy current loss (reduced by laminated core), (3) hysteresis loss, (4) flux leakage.
  • No violation: voltage goes up but current goes down in the same ratio; power out ≤ power in.
  • Numerical: Vs = 90 × 3000/200 = 1350 V. Ip = Is × Ns/Np = 2 × 15 = 30 A.
  • Works only on ac (dc gives no changing flux) – asked 2015.

q: Q63. (3 marks) Name the EM waves used for (a) radar/aircraft navigation (b) treating muscular strain (physiotherapy) (c) diagnosis of bone fracture (d) water purification / LASIK eye surgery. How are they produced? [2015, 2018, 2019; 2016, 2017 similar]
a: Answer: (a) Microwaves – klystron, magnetron, Gunn diode. (b) Infrared – hot bodies, vibrating molecules. (c) X-rays – fast electrons hitting a metal target. (d) Ultraviolet – very hot bodies, sun, special lamps. Order of increasing frequency: radio < microwave < infrared < visible < UV < X-ray < gamma.

q: Q64. (3 marks) What is displacement current? Where does it exist while a capacitor is charging? [2025; 2017, 2016]
a: Answer: Id = ε0 dΦE/dt – a current due to a changing electric field (no charges move). While charging, conduction current flows in the wires; between the plates there is no conduction current, but E is changing, so displacement current exists there. Id = conduction current, so current is continuous. In steady state ΦE is constant → no current.

q: Q65. (MCQ) Electric field amplitude of an EM wave in free space is 1000 V/m. Magnetic field amplitude = ? [2025]
Q66. (Numerical, 2 marks) E = 30 sin(2π × 10^18 t + π × 10^10 x), B = 10^-7 sin(same). Find refractive index of the medium, frequency, and name the wave. [SQP]
a: Steps: v = ω/k = 2π × 10^18 / (π × 10^10) = 2 × 10^8 m/s. n = c/v = 1.5. f = ω/2π = 10^18 Hz → X-rays. (Wave travels along −x.)

q: Q67. (2 marks) Write three characteristics of EM waves. [2025, 2026]
a: Answer: (1) Transverse – E and B perpendicular to each other and to direction of travel. (2) Travel in vacuum with speed c = 1/√(μ0ε0) = 3 × 10^8 m/s. (3) E0/B0 = c; they carry energy and momentum; no medium needed.

chapter: Chapter 9 – Ray Optics and Optical Instruments
q: Q68. (Numerical, 2 marks) Object 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of radius 40 cm. Find image position and magnification. [2024]
a: Steps: f = −20 cm, u = −30 cm. 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = −1/20 + 1/30 = −1/60 → v = −60 cm (real, in front). m = −v/u = −(−60)/(−30) = −2 → real, inverted, twice as big.

chapter: Chapter 9 – Ray Optics and Optical Instruments
q: Q69. (Numerical, 2 marks) A convex lens of focal length 20 cm forms the image of an object 30 cm away. Position and nature? [2026]
a: Steps: u = −30, f = +20. 1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/20 − 1/30 = 1/60 → v = +60 cm. m = v/u = −2 → real, inverted, magnified, on the other side.

chapter: Chapter 9 – Ray Optics and Optical Instruments
q: Q70. (Numerical, 2 marks) A plano-convex lens of focal length 16 cm is made of material n = 1.4. Radius of the curved surface? [2024]

chapter: Chapter 9 – Ray Optics and Optical Instruments
q: Q71. (Numerical, 2 marks) An equiconvex lens of glass n = 1.55 has f = 15 cm. Radius of each surface? [2025; 2017 had f = 20 cm]

chapter: Chapter 9 – Ray Optics and Optical Instruments
q: Q72. (Derivation, 5 marks) Derive n2/v − n1/u = (n2 − n1)/R for refraction at a convex spherical surface; hence derive the lens maker's formula. [2015, 2016, 2023, 2026]
a:
Steps:

  1. Point object O in medium n1 on axis; convex surface (centre C, radius R) into medium n2; image I. Ray ON hits surface at N, refracts along NI. Angles with axis: α (at O), β (at I), γ (at C). Small angles.
  2. In triangles: i = α + γ, r = γ − β.
  3. Snell (small angles): n1 i = n2 r → n1(α + γ) = n2(γ − β).
  4. With tan ≈ angle: α = MN/OM, β = MN/MI, γ = MN/MC.
  5. n1/OM + n2/MI = (n2 − n1)/MC. Signs: OM = −u, MI = +v, MC = +R → n2/v − n1/u = (n2 − n1)/R.
  6. Lens: first surface (R1) forms image I1 at v1: n2/v1 − n1/u = (n2 − n1)/R1. I1 is object for second surface (R2): n1/v − n2/v1 = (n1 − n2)/R2.
  7. Add: n1(1/v − 1/u) = (n2 − n1)(1/R1 − 1/R2). For object at infinity v = f:
  8. 1/f = (n21 − 1)(1/R1 − 1/R2), n21 = n2/n1.

chapter: Chapter 9 – Ray Optics and Optical Instruments
q: Q73. (Numerical, 2 marks) Light from a point source in air falls on a convex glass surface (n = 1.5, R = 20 cm). Source is 100 cm away. Find image position. [2016]

chapter: Chapter 9 – Ray Optics and Optical Instruments
q: Q74. (3 marks) State conditions for total internal reflection and relate critical angle to n. A ray inside diamond (n = 2.42) hits the surface at 30°. Refraction or TIR? Why do diamonds sparkle? [SQP; 2016, 2018, 2019, 2023, 2026]
a: Answer: Conditions: (1) light goes from denser to rarer medium; (2) angle of incidence > critical angle. sin C = 1/n. Diamond: sin C = 1/2.42 = 0.413 → C ≈ 24.4°. 30° > 24.4° → total internal reflection. Diamonds are cut so light undergoes many TIRs inside before coming out → sparkle. Other uses: optical fibres, prisms in binoculars. (Twinkling of stars is due to refraction, not TIR – 2026 MCQ.)

chapter: Chapter 9 – Ray Optics and Optical Instruments
q: Q75. (Numerical, 3 marks) Prism of refractive index √2 and angle 60°. Find angle of minimum deviation and angle of incidence. Draw the i–δ graph. [2024; 2025, 2017, 2019]
a: Steps: n = sin[(A + Dm)/2] / sin(A/2). √2 = sin[(60 + Dm)/2] / sin 30° → sin[(60 + Dm)/2] = √2 × 0.5 = 1/√2 → (60 + Dm)/2 = 45° → Dm = 30°. At minimum deviation i = (A + Dm)/2 = 45°. Graph: δ vs i is a U-shaped curve; its lowest point is Dm (at Dm, ray passes symmetrically, i = e, r1 = r2 = A/2).

chapter: Chapter 9 – Ray Optics and Optical Instruments
q: Q76. (Numerical, 3 marks) A compound microscope: fo = 2 cm, fe = 5 cm, object 2.2 cm from objective. Find (i) image by objective (ii) magnifying power with final image at infinity. [SQP]

chapter: Chapter 9 – Ray Optics and Optical Instruments
q: Q77. (Numerical, 3 marks) Telescope: objective 15 m, eyepiece 1.0 cm. (i) angular magnification (ii) diameter of the Moon's image by objective (Moon diameter 3.48 × 10^6 m, orbit radius 3.8 × 10^8 m). Draw the ray diagram (normal adjustment). Why large objective aperture? [2015, 2019; 2016, 2017, 2026 MCQ (fo = 144 cm, fe = 6 cm → m = 24, tube length 150 cm)]
a: Steps: (i) m = fo/fe = 1500/1 = 1500. (ii) angle subtended by Moon α = 3.48 × 10^6 / 3.8 × 10^8; image size = fo × α = 15 × 9.16 × 10^-3 ≈ 0.137 m = 13.7 cm. Large aperture: gathers more light (bright image) and gives higher resolving power. Objective: large f; eyepiece: small f. Near-point adjustment: m = (fo/fe)(1 + fe/D). Reflecting telescope advantages: no chromatic aberration, cheaper large mirror, more light, better resolution.

chapter: Chapter 9 – Ray Optics and Optical Instruments
q: Q78. (MCQ set) (a) Two convex lenses of 60 cm and 20 cm in contact: power? (b) An equiconvex lens of power P is cut into two halves perpendicular to the axis: power of each part? (c) Convex lens immersed in water: focal length? Derive 1/f = 1/f1 + 1/f2. [2024 case; 2017, 2026 derivation; SQP A-R] Answers: (a) P = 1/0.6 + 1/0.2 = 1.67 + 5 = 6.67 D. (b) Each half is plano-convex with one curved face → P/2. (c) Increases (relative refractive index n(glass)/n(water) is smaller, so (n − 1) term smaller).
a: Derivation: Lens 1 alone: 1/v1 − 1/u = 1/f1. Image of lens 1 is object for lens 2 (in contact): 1/v − 1/v1 = 1/f2. Add: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f1 + 1/f2 = 1/f. So P = P1 + P2.

q: Q79. (Derivation, 3 marks) Using Huygens' principle, derive Snell's law of refraction. Which prediction of wave theory was later verified? [SQP; 2017, 2019 (or), 2016]
a:
Steps:

  1. Plane wavefront AB (in medium 1, speed v1) strikes surface PP' at angle i. While B travels BC = v1t to reach the surface at C, a secondary wavelet from A travels AE = v2t in medium 2.
  2. Tangent CE from C to the wavelet (radius v2t) is the refracted wavefront, at angle r.
  3. In triangle ABC: sin i = BC/AC = v1t/AC. In triangle AEC: sin r = AE/AC = v2t/AC.
  4. sin i / sin r = v1/v2 = constant = n21 (= n2/n1) → Snell's law.
  5. Prediction: speed of light in a denser medium is less than in air (v2 < v1 when light bends towards normal) – later verified experimentally (Foucault). Diagram: incident wavefront AB, surface, arc of radius v2t from A, refracted wavefront EC.

q: Q80. (Derivation, 3 marks) State Huygens' principle; prove i = r for reflection using it. [2018, 2019, 2024]
a: Answer: Huygens: (1) every point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets moving with the wave's speed; (2) the forward envelope (common tangent) of these wavelets gives the new wavefront. Proof: Wavefront AB hits mirror at A. In time t, B reaches C (BC = vt). Wavelet from A has radius AE = vt. Tangent CE is the reflected wavefront. Triangles ABC and CEA are congruent (common AC, right angles at B and E, BC = AE) → i = r.

q: Q81. (A-R) YDSE: d = 0.25 mm, D = 1.0 m, λ = 500 nm. A: fringe width is 2.0 mm. R: fringe width is directly proportional to slit separation and inversely to wavelength. [SQP]
Q82. (Numerical, 2 marks) In YDSE, light has a known wavelength 520 nm and an unknown λ'. The 4th bright fringe of λ' coincides with the 5th bright fringe of 520 nm. Find λ'. [2024]
a: Steps: Bright fringe position y = nλD/d. 4λ'D/d = 5 × 520 × D/d → λ' = 650 nm.

q: Q83. (Numerical, 2 marks) Two coherent beams of intensities I and 4I superpose. Find Imax/Imin. [2023; 2018 similar]
a: Steps: Amplitude ∝ √I: a1 = 1, a2 = 2 (in units). Imax ∝ (2 + 1)² = 9, Imin ∝ (2 − 1)² = 1 → 9 : 1.

q: Q84. (2 marks) What are coherent sources? Can two independent sodium lamps be coherent? Why is sustained interference needed? [2024]
a: Answer: Sources with the same frequency and a constant phase difference. Two independent lamps cannot be coherent – each emits from millions of atoms whose phases change randomly about every 10^-8 s, so the pattern shifts too fast to see. Coherent sources are made from one source (e.g. two slits lit by one source).

q: Q85. (3 marks) A YDSE set-up in water is moved to a liquid of higher refractive index. Effect on (a) speed, frequency, wavelength of light (b) fringe width, shape, position of central maximum. [2025]
a: Answer: (a) Speed decreases, frequency unchanged, wavelength decreases. (b) Fringe width β = λD/d decreases; fringes remain straight lines; central maximum stays at the same place (centre).

q: Q86. (Numerical, 2 marks) A teacher uses a 633 nm laser; screen 5.0 m away; wants fringe width 5 mm. Slit separation? [2026]
Q87. (2–3 marks) Give two differences between interference and diffraction patterns. In single-slit diffraction, what happens to the central band if slit width is doubled? [2017, 2018, 2019, 2023]
a: Answer: Interference: superposition of waves from two coherent sources; fringes of equal width; all bright fringes equally bright. Diffraction: superposition of wavelets from different parts of the same wavefront; central maximum twice as wide as others; brightness falls quickly away from centre. Doubling slit width: central band width (2λD/a) halves; it becomes brighter (more light passes, energy in a smaller area). Diffraction of sound is common because its wavelength (≈ 1 m) is comparable to doors/obstacles, while light's wavelength is very small (2026 Q).

chapter: Chapter 11 – Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
q: Q88. (3 marks) Write Einstein's photoelectric equation. Explain using photon picture: (a) threshold frequency (b) Kmax independent of intensity (c) V0 vs ν is a straight line of slope h/e. [2025; 2015, 2017, 2019, SQP]
a: Answer: hν = φ0 + Kmax, i.e. Kmax = hν − φ0 = eV0. (a) One photon frees one electron. If hν < φ0 (ν < ν0 = φ0/h), no electron can escape however intense the light. (b) Intensity = number of photons; it increases current, not energy per photon. Kmax depends only on ν. (c) eV0 = hν − φ0 → V0 = (h/e)ν − φ0/e: straight line, slope h/e (same for all metals), intercept on ν-axis = ν0. Also: emission is instantaneous – wave theory cannot explain (a), (b) or this.

chapter: Chapter 11 – Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
q: Q89. (MCQ) Radiation of 200 nm falls on a surface of work function 4.2 eV. Kmax ≈ ? [2026]

chapter: Chapter 11 – Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
q: Q90. (MCQ) Photons of 3.3 eV and 11.3 eV fall on a metal (φ = 2.3 eV). Ratio of maximum speeds of electrons? [2024]

chapter: Chapter 11 – Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
q: Q91. (Graphs, 3 marks) Plot (a) photocurrent vs collector plate potential for two intensities (same frequency) (b) same for two frequencies (same intensity) (c) photocurrent vs intensity. [2023; 2017, 2018]
a: Answer: (a) Two curves with the same stopping potential (same point on negative axis) but different saturation currents – higher intensity, higher saturation. (b) Same saturation current, higher frequency → more negative stopping potential. (c) Straight line through the origin (current ∝ intensity).

chapter: Chapter 11 – Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
q: Q92. (MCQ) An electron and a proton have the same de Broglie wavelength. They have the same: momentum / speed / energy / angular momentum? [2024]
a: Answer: Momentum (λ = h/p).

chapter: Chapter 11 – Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
q: Q93. (MCQ) A proton and an alpha particle have equal momentum. Ratio of their kinetic energies Kp/Kα and wavelengths λp/λα? [2026]
a: Steps: K = p²/2m → Kp/Kα = mα/mp = 4. λ = h/p → λp/λα = 1. Answer: 4, 1.

chapter: Chapter 11 – Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
q: Q94. (2 marks) De Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through 100 V? [Practice; 2019 asked the λ vs 1/√V graph]
a: Steps: λ = h/√(2meV) = 1.227/√V nm = 1.227/10 = 0.123 nm. Graph λ vs 1/√V is a straight line through origin with slope h/√(2mq): smaller slope means larger charge (for same mass).

chapter: Chapter 11 – Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
q: Q95. (2 marks) A neutron (mass m) of kinetic energy E and a photon of the same energy. Find λn/λp. [2024]
a: Steps: λn = h/√(2mE). λp = hc/E. λn/λp = E / (c√(2mE)) = √(E/(2mc²)) = (1/c)√(E/2m).

chapter: Chapter 11 – Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
q: Q96. (MCQ) Red and blue beams have equal intensity. Which is true? [2025]
a: Answer: The red beam has more photons (each red photon has less energy, so more photons are needed for the same intensity). Photons and electrons both show dual nature.

q: Q97. (2 marks) State Bohr's quantisation condition. How does de Broglie's hypothesis explain it? [SQP; 2018]
a: Answer: mvr = nh/2π (angular momentum is a whole-number multiple of h/2π); electrons in these orbits do not radiate. De Broglie: electron is a wave, λ = h/mv. A stable orbit holds a standing wave, so circumference = nλ: 2πr = nh/mv → mvr = nh/2π.

q: Q98. (Derivation, 3 marks) Show that radius of nth Bohr orbit ∝ n² (also give v and E). [2015; 2023 MCQ]
a:
Steps:

  1. Centripetal force = Coulomb force: mv²/r = ke²/r².
  2. Bohr: mvr = nh/2π → v = nh/(2πmr).
  3. Substitute: m[n²h²/(4π²m²r²)]/r = ke²/r² → r = n²h²/(4π²mke²) = ε0n²h²/(πme²).
  4. So rn ∝ n² (r1 = 0.53 Å). vn = 2πke²/(nh) ∝ 1/n. En = −13.6/n² eV.
  5. Total energy E = −ke²/2r; KE = +ke²/2r; PE = −ke²/r (2025 case).

q: Q99. (Numerical, 2 marks) Ground-state energy of H is −13.6 eV. Find KE and PE in the third excited state. [2023]
a: Steps: Third excited state = n = 4. E = −13.6/16 = −0.85 eV. KE = −E = 0.85 eV. PE = 2E = −1.70 eV.

q: Q100. (Numerical, 2 marks) H atom in ground state absorbs a photon and goes to n = 4. Frequency of photon? [2018; 2023 (n = 5)]
Q101. (Numerical, 2 marks) An electron jumps from −1.51 eV to −3.4 eV. Wavelength emitted and series? [2017]
a: Steps: ΔE = 1.89 eV. λ = 1240/1.89 ≈ 656 nm (red). −1.51 eV is n = 3, −3.4 eV is n = 2 → Balmer series (visible).

q: Q102. (MCQ) The second line of the Balmer series in H corresponds to the transition: [2024]
a: Answer: ni = 4 → nf = 2. (First line: 3 → 2.) Series: Lyman (to n = 1, UV), Balmer (to n = 2, visible), Paschen (to n = 3, IR) – energy-level diagram asked 2023.

q: Q103. (A-R / 3 marks) Rutherford's α-scattering: why do most α-particles pass undeflected? Give drawbacks of Rutherford's model and how Bohr removed them. [SQP (A-R answer B); 2024; 2015]
a: Answer: Most of the atom is empty space; the positive charge and mass are in a tiny nucleus (≈ 10^-15 m vs atom ≈ 10^-10 m). (In the SQP A-R, both statements are true but R is not the correct reason → B.) Drawbacks: (1) an accelerating (revolving) electron should radiate energy, spiral into the nucleus – atom would be unstable; (2) it predicts a continuous spectrum, but hydrogen gives a line spectrum. Bohr: electrons move only in certain stationary orbits without radiating; radiation is emitted only during a jump, hν = Ei − Ef. Ionisation energy of H = 13.6 eV (SQP).

q: Q104. (Numerical, 3 marks) Atomic mass of O-16 is 15.99493 u. mp = 1.00727 u, mn = 1.00866 u, 1 u = 931.5 MeV. Find binding energy per nucleon. [SQP]
Q105. (Derivation, 2–3 marks) Using R = R0 A^(1/3), show nuclear density is the same for all nuclei. [2015, 2019, 2023, 2024]
a: Steps: Mass ≈ mA (m = mass of a nucleon). Volume = (4/3)πR³ = (4/3)πR0³A. Density = mA / [(4/3)πR0³A] = 3m/(4πR0³) – no A, so same for all nuclei (≈ 2.3 × 10^17 kg/m³). Nuclear density >> atomic density because nearly all mass is packed in a tiny nucleus. 2026 MCQ: r1/r2 for A = 64 and 27 = (64/27)^(1/3) = 4/3.

q: Q106. (3 marks) Draw the BE/A vs mass number curve. Give two features. Why do light nuclei fuse and heavy nuclei split? [2023, 2018; SQP MCQ]
a: Answer: Curve rises steeply for light nuclei, peaks at about 8.75 MeV near A = 56 (iron – most stable), then falls slowly to about 7.6 MeV at A = 238. Features: (1) nearly constant (≈ 8 MeV) for A = 30–170 – nuclear force is short-range (saturation); (2) lower for very light and very heavy nuclei. Fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy nuclei both move towards higher BE/A, so energy is released.

q: Q107. (3 marks) Differentiate between nuclear fission and fusion with one example each. [2026; 2015]
a: Answer: Fission – a heavy nucleus splits into two medium nuclei: 235U + 1n → 144Ba + 89Kr + 3 1n + about 200 MeV. Happens with slow neutrons, used in reactors. Fusion – light nuclei join to form a heavier one: 2H + 3H → 4He + 1n + 17.6 MeV. Needs very high temperature (~10^7 K), powers the Sun.

q: Q108. (2 marks) Define mass defect and binding energy. Give two properties of nuclear force. [2026; 2024]
a: Answer: Mass defect Δm = (Zmp + Nmn) − M(nucleus). Binding energy = Δm c² = energy needed to separate the nucleus into its nucleons. Nuclear force: very strong (much stronger than Coulomb), short range (a few fm), charge-independent, attractive at 0.8–2 fm but repulsive below about 0.8 fm. (2026 A-R "nuclear forces are always attractive / R: nuclear force is weak" → both false → D.)

q: Q109. (3 marks) Draw energy band diagrams of a conductor, insulator and semiconductor. Why is diamond an insulator but tin a conductor (both group IV)? Why is Si used, not diamond? [SQP; 2025 MCQ (Sn conducts)]
a: Answer: Conductor – valence and conduction bands overlap (or partly filled conduction band). Insulator – large gap Eg > 3 eV (diamond 5.4 eV). Semiconductor – small gap, Eg < 3 eV (Si 1.1 eV, Ge 0.7 eV). Diamond's gap is too big for thermal excitation at room temperature; in tin the bands overlap so free electrons are available. Silicon's small gap lets electrons cross with thermal energy, and conduction can be controlled by doping.

q: Q110. (2 marks) Distinguish intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors. How are charge carriers created in an intrinsic semiconductor? [2015, 2023, 2026]
a: Answer: Intrinsic: pure; ne = nh = ni; conductivity depends only on temperature. Extrinsic: doped; ne ≠ nh; conductivity depends on doping and temperature. In intrinsic, thermal energy breaks some covalent bonds; each freed electron goes to the conduction band and leaves a hole in the valence band (electron-hole pairs).

q: Q111. (2 marks) Ge is doped with arsenic. What type is formed? What are majority/minority carriers in n- and p-type? [2024 MCQ; 2025, 2023]
a: Answer: As is pentavalent (donor) → n-type; number of conduction electrons increases. n-type: majority electrons, minority holes. p-type (trivalent dopant: B, Al, Ga, In – acceptor): majority holes, minority electrons. Even so, n-type is electrically neutral (each donor ion is positive, balancing the extra electron) – 2025 A-R answer (A). Donor level is about 0.01 eV (Ge) to 0.05 eV (Si) below the conduction band (2023 MCQ: order 0.01 eV).

q: Q112. (Numerical, 2 marks) Pure Si has ni = 1.5 × 10^16 m^-3. On doping, hole concentration becomes 4.5 × 10^22 m^-3. Identify dopant type and find electron concentration. [Type seen 2025; NCERT values]
a: Steps: Holes increase → trivalent (acceptor) dopant → p-type. ne × nh = ni² → ne = (1.5 × 10^16)² / 4.5 × 10^22 = 2.25 × 10^32 / 4.5 × 10^22 = 5 × 10^9 m^-3.

q: Q113. (3 marks) Explain formation of depletion region and potential barrier in a p-n junction (role of diffusion and drift currents). [2016, 2023, 2025]
a: Answer: Electrons diffuse from n to p and holes from p to n (concentration difference) → diffusion current (p to n). They leave behind fixed positive donor ions on the n-side and fixed negative acceptor ions on the p-side near the junction → a layer with no free carriers = depletion region. These ions set up an electric field from n to p, which pushes minority carriers across → drift current (n to p). At equilibrium diffusion current = drift current; the potential difference across the layer is the barrier potential (≈ 0.7 V Si, 0.3 V Ge). Diagram: p | depletion layer (− ions on p side, + ions on n side) | n, with field arrow from n to p.

q: Q114. (3 marks) With circuit diagrams, explain forward and reverse bias. Draw the V–I characteristic of a Si diode. [2026, 2023]
a: Answer: Forward bias: p to + terminal, n to −. Barrier and depletion width decrease; current rises sharply after about 0.7 V (knee/threshold voltage); current in mA. Reverse bias: p to −, n to +. Barrier and depletion width increase; tiny reverse current (μA) due to minority carriers, almost constant until breakdown. Graph: forward curve in first quadrant rising steeply after 0.7 V; reverse curve in third quadrant almost flat and close to the axis. Minority carrier injection happens in forward bias (2026 MCQ). Forward resistance = ΔV/ΔI, e.g. (1.0 − 0.8) V / 2 mA = 100 Ω (2026 MCQ).

q: Q115. (3 marks) Draw a full-wave rectifier circuit and explain its working with input and output waveforms. What is the output ripple frequency for 50 Hz input in half-wave and full-wave? [2017, 2018, 2019, 2024 case; 2016 half-wave]
a: Answer: Centre-tap transformer, two diodes D1, D2 and load RL. In the first half cycle top end A is +ve: D1 forward biased conducts, D2 reverse biased; current through RL in one direction. In the next half, B is +ve: D2 conducts, D1 off; current through RL in the same direction. So both halves give output in one direction – pulsating dc. At any instant one diode is forward and the other reverse biased (2024 MCQ); each diode conducts for half a cycle. Half-wave (one diode) gives output only in alternate half cycles. Ripple frequency: half-wave 50 Hz, full-wave 100 Hz. Waveforms: input sine; half-wave output = only positive humps with gaps; full-wave output = continuous positive humps.
